name: Togo
summary_text: Togo criminalises consensual same-sex sexual activity between men and between women. The provision is the Penal Code offence of "acts against nature committed with an individual of one's sex", punishable by up to three years' imprisonment and a fine (Human Dignity Trust).  The United States Department of State's 2023 Country Report on Human Rights Practices states that the same law also prohibits "promotion of same-sex conduct", a clause understood to reach advocacy and gender identity expression, and records that the provision was enforced during the reporting period. Because the offence is drafted in terms of sexual acts rather than identity, a trans visitor's exposure is not self-evident from the code alone; the practical risk attaches to visibility, conduct and advocacy, and the sources do not delimit where the promotion clause ends.  Violence or threats of violence targeting LGBTTQI persons were listed among significant human-rights issues in Togo's 2023 human rights report, and the 2022 report carried the same finding. The 2011 report for Togo separately documented official and societal discrimination against lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender people alongside security-force torture and impunity, indicating a pattern recorded across more than a decade of external reporting.  A 2015 Washington Blade account of interviews conducted in March 2015 describes Lomé's police as "particularly merciless when dealing with LGBT locals and tourists", and recounts the author's return to the site of a 2008 attack on him in the capital. This is a direct on-the-ground assertion of tourist exposure to policing in Lomé rather than a general crime observation.  An alternative report submitted to the United Nations Human Rights Committee in June 2021 by AAEC Togo and Synergia describes an active civil-society channel: the Togolese association works on HIV within MSM-TG populations under the National Strategic Plan 2016-2020, documents LGBT rights violations across Togo and francophone West Africa, and provides legal and judicial support to victims.

sources.title: New Penal Code (2015), Article 393
sources.documents: Revised criminalization phrasing to 'indecent or unnatural act committed with a person of the same sex'; retains 1-3 years imprisonment, increases fine to 1 to 3 million CFA francs
sources.detail: Cited in text as 'In 2015, a new Penal Code was adopted' and 'Article 393'; no URL visible

name: Thailand
summary_text: The Immigration Bureau runs 'Welcome Pride by Immigration', launched on 5 August 2024, which addresses the concerns of foreign LGBTQ+ travellers whose passports do not match their current appearance or gender and eases immigration scrutiny on arrival. It is the one entry-side accommodation a trans visitor can rely on before landing.  Same-sex marriage has been legal since 22 January 2025, after the bill passed its final Senate reading in June 2024, making Thailand the first country in Southeast Asia to do so; the statute uses gender-neutral 'marriage partners' terms. Couples who married after that date gain access to property regimes, succession, hospital visitation and pension survivor claims from which they were previously excluded.  Legal gender recognition remains absent. There is no mechanism to change the sex marker on a birth certificate, national ID card or passport, and official title prefixes are fixed to the sex recorded at birth, so a trans woman's documents may still carry a male honorific. The Name Act 1962 offers only a partial workaround through first-name change, and even that leaves final discretion with officials. A 2021 Human Rights Watch report, 'People Can't Be Fit into Boxes', documented the absence of any route to documentation reflecting gender identity and found that anti-discrimination protections are not fully enforced. Anti-discrimination law has existed since 2015. At a 2025 'Pride in Action' forum at Lido Connect, advocates urged the government to expedite a gender-recognition law after marriage equality, confirming that recognition legislation was still pending.  Thai law carries no hate-crime designation. In April 2025 a Chinese tourist murdered a trans woman in Pattaya after she refused his request for sex; the perpetrator was named in domestic reporting as 42-year-old Fu Tongyung. The community described the killing as a hate crime, but bias-motivated violence is prosecuted as an ordinary offence with no enhanced penalties and no collection of bias-crime data, and LGBTQ+ groups subsequently called for new hate-crime protections. The gap is an accountability problem a trans visitor should weigh when assessing how a violent incident involving them would be classified.  Detention carries documented risk. The Department of Corrections states that LGBT prisoners have been separated from other inmates nationwide since 1993, and at Pattaya Remand Prison transgender inmates are held in a dedicated block apart from cisgender men; of roughly 300,000 Thai prisoners, more than 6,000 were registered as sexual minorities. Trans woman Theerayut Charoenpakdee, stopped by police in 2017 and expecting to be held with men because her documents still carried the title 'Mr.', was instead placed in the separated wing. The pattern is uneven: trans activist Nachacha Kongudom, arrested in June 2015 while protesting the junta, was sent to a men's prison against her request, where officials told her that under Thai law 'she remains a man' and no Thai document can identify a trans woman as female, and where she was harassed at intake and ordered to expose her body. The Department of Corrections then announced a pilot using Bangkok's Min Buri prison as an LGBT facility; activists insisted placement should be an option rather than an obligation and warned that segregation could encourage exclusion. Reporting from 2016 also noted that transgender women outside such units usually face a choice between men's cells and solitary confinement.

sources.title: Gender Equality Act B.E. 2558
sources.documents: Thailand's comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation and gender identity; bans discrimination against male, female or 'a person who has a sexual expression different from that person's original sex' with penalty up to 6 months prison and 20,000 baht fine, with exception for 'education, religion and the public interest'
sources.detail: Cited as Gender Equality Act B.E. 2558 (Thai: พระราชบัญญัติความเท่าเทียมระหว่างเพศ พ.ศ.๒๕๕๘) passed 13 March 2015, came into force 9 September 2015. No URL visible in provided text.

sources.title: Marriage Equality Act - Amendment to Civil and Commercial Code
sources.documents: Legalization of same-sex marriage and joint adoption by married same-sex couples; replaces terms 'men and women' and 'husband and wife' with 'individuals' and 'spouses'
sources.detail: Cited as passed House 27 March 2024 and Senate 18 June 2024, endorsed by King Maha Vajiralongkorn, published in Royal Gazette 24 September 2024, effective 23 January 2025. No URL visible in provided text.

sources.title: Constitutional Court ruling 2021 on Section 1448 Civil and Commercial Code
sources.documents: Ruled that Section 1448 interpreting marriages as only between women and men is constitutional; full ruling contained language describing LGBTQ people as unable to reproduce, against nature, different 'species' incapable of creating 'delicate bond'
sources.detail: Cited as 2021 Constitutional Court ruling on Section 1448. No URL visible in provided text.
